The central question is whether a shared multilingual model can simultaneously serve languages whose scripts, morphologies, and typological structures differ so radically that the subword vocabulary, attention topology, and parameter capacity become sites of zero-sum competition rather than positive transfer. The key concepts are: script-distance asymmetry (the tokenizer's fertility diverges sharply across scripts — a single Arabic word may tokenize into 1–2 pieces while its Turkish translation yields 6–8, meaning Turkish "uses more model" per semantic unit), shared subword space pollution (fine-tuning on high-resource Latin-script data reshapes the embedding geometry that low-resource Cyrillic or Indic languages depend on, because subword overlap is sparse but gradient flow is not isolated), per-language capacity starvation (each transformer layer has fixed parameter count regardless of how many languages compete for representational slots, so minority-language features get overwritten rather than consolidated), and catastrophic interference (gradient updates from one language's fine-tuning loss directly corrupt weight configurations that supported another language, with no architectural gate preventing it). What a beginner misses is that the damage is asymmetric and non-obvious: high-resource dominant-script languages appear fine on aggregate benchmarks while low-resource languages silently collapse, and the collapse is not uniform — phonologically rich or morphologically agglutinative languages lose inflectional accuracy first, while coarser semantic tasks survive longer, creating a false impression of retained capability. An expert worries specifically about the interaction between tokenizer fertility imbalance and gradient magnitude: languages with higher fertility produce larger, noisier gradient signals per sample, effectively giving them disproportionate influence over shared layer weights even when sampling is balanced by document count.

Temperature-based sampling (the canonical form being the α=0.7 smoothing used in mBERT and XLM, and later in mT5's training regime) corrects for data volume disparity — it upsamples low-resource languages so they appear more frequently in training batches, partially offsetting the dominance of English and Chinese by document count. Loss-weighted schemes go slightly further by reweighting the gradient contribution per sample, which can partially compensate for the fact that a high-fertility language like Tamil produces more cross-entropy signal per sentence simply because it has more tokens to predict. What both approaches leave entirely untouched is the per-token embedding gradient asymmetry: a Tamil sentence with fertility 2.3× that of its English translation still produces 2.3× the gradient flow through the shared embedding matrix per semantic unit, regardless of how often that sentence is sampled — sampling frequency and per-sample gradient magnitude are orthogonal axes. Neither scheme touches layer-wise capacity allocation: the same 12 or 24 transformer layers must simultaneously encode morphological paradigms for agglutinative languages (Finnish, Turkish, Swahili) and the sparser, positional syntax of isolating languages (Mandarin, Vietnamese), with no mechanism to route language-specific features to dedicated capacity. Pfeiffer et al. (2022) in their MAD-X framework demonstrated this explicitly: even with balanced sampling, adapter-free multilingual fine-tuning on NER caused Swahili and Yoruba to degrade relative to their pretrained baselines, because fine-tuning reshaped shared layers in ways sampling could not prevent. The deepest untouched bias is subword identity collision: when two languages share a subword surface form with divergent semantic roles (e.g., the piece "-ing" appears in English gerunds and in Yoruba morpheme boundaries), sampling does nothing to disentangle their embeddings — both gradient streams update the same vector in conflicting directions, and the model has no signal that a collision is occurring.

Language-ID prepending works by injecting a language-specific token (e.g., [EN], [SW], [AR]) at position 0, whose embedding the model learns to use as a context-setting bias vector that propagates through attention into every subsequent layer — in practice, the language-ID token attends broadly and its value vector additively shifts the residual stream of ambiguous subword representations toward a language-specific manifold. The mechanism is therefore not resolution but conditional routing: the embedding for "-ing" remains a single contaminated vector in the weight matrix, but the attention pattern over the language-ID token's output nudges downstream representations so that the final hidden states diverge by language even when the input subwords are identical. The masking is most visible in probing studies: Libovický et al. (2020) showed that subword embeddings in mBERT encode language identity weakly at the embedding layer but increasingly strongly in upper layers, which is precisely what you'd expect if language-ID context is being injected via attention rather than by disentangling the embedding vectors themselves. In mBART, where language-ID appears at both encoder input and decoder start, the mechanism additionally gates generation mode — the decoder's initial hidden state is seeded with the target-language token, which biases the output distribution toward target-script subwords early in decoding, partially suppressing cross-lingual lexical bleed. The critical failure mode this masking produces is context-length sensitivity: on short inputs (1–3 tokens), the language-ID signal has insufficient attention budget to fully condition all positions, and collision artifacts resurface — Wu & Dredze (2020) observed disproportionate degradation on short multilingual sequences in mBERT fine-tuning, consistent with this attention-dilution account. At inference time on an out-of-distribution language (one seen in pretraining but absent from fine-tuning), the language-ID token activates a pretrained routing pathway that fine-tuning never updated, meaning the model applies the contaminated fine-tuned weights without the compensating layer-wise adjustments that fine-tuning would have induced — this is the precise mechanism behind zero-shot cross-lingual transfer degradation, not mere vocabulary mismatch.

Direct evidence for dynamic freeze scheduling in multilingual fine-tuning is sparse, but the closest empirical work comes from curricula and layer-wise adaptive rate methods: Ro et al. A subtler failure mode is monitoring language selection bias: if the alignment probe set is drawn from the fine-tuning language or typologically similar languages, the signal will appear stable while distant languages silently degrade, because the geometric drift that damages Swahili or Tamil representations may be orthogonal to the subspace the probe is measuring.
